993.t: Avant-garde and free jazz labels; Sam Rivers and structure that emerges
993.s: Daley rejects the labels and describes spontaneous composition with Sam Rivers.
993.q: Well avante garde means, you know, new, cutting edge. But this is music that has been played since 1971 you know. So I mean it’s not new anymore. So avant garde is a term — just to put it in a box and everything. And free jazz, if you listen to Sam Rivers and other very sophisticated progressive…

993.s: The trio does not abandon tradition; Sam Rivers knew the standards.
993.q: There’s no such thing as a silly question. I taught school for 30 years, every student. I said there’s no such thing as a silly question.

531.s: Prompted by Roscoe Mitchell's remark, she says she cannot define free music but still gravitates to structure.
531.ch: Her music, free jazz and playing
531.q: I guess we’re freeing ourselves from playing, from doing these things like playing rhythm, playing melody, playing harmony, in that certain way but we still use time, we still use rhythm and melody and harmony but just not in a preconceived way I guess. But when I play free music I always tend, I…

531.t: Karl Berger's view and free recording with Friedman and Mondlak
531.s: Self-imposed guidelines in free music; she recorded a free CD with David Friedman and her husband without discussion.
531.ch: Her music, free jazz and playing
531.q: That’s a nice way to say it. There are guidelines and they are self-imposed and people just don’t know what the guideline is going to be at that moment, that they’re shifting guidelines maybe and you don’t agree on them necessarily. Everybody can have their own or you go with the other person’s…

140.s: Asked if they discussed the new music, both say it happened spontaneously on the bandstand as evolution from bebop.
140.q: No we didn’t, I didn’t, we didn’t ever really talk about it. We just did it. It was like, I mean for me, and the guys I was hanging out with, you know we didn’t sit down and say now we’re going to play in or we’re going to play out or we going to try and play without bars, you know. It was just…

116.t: Free jazz experiences, including the Eddie Harris duo 'Homecoming'
116.s: He played a totally free concert with a visiting altoist and recorded a partly free duo with Eddie Harris.
116.q: I think I did once on a live concert. It was an alto saxophone player who came through New Orleans and I was in the rhythm section. And what was his name — he’s still on the faculty at Oberlin.

845.t: Time in free improvisation and Charles Tolliver's band
845.s: He explains how time exists in free playing, citing Tolliver's big band, and the college rule against jazz in practice rooms.
845.ch: Free playing, time and the Classic Jazz Trio
845.q: But that’s what I mean, you apply yourself to the situation and so therefore what the definition, how you define time, is different than how you define time in a twelve bar blues. This might be longer or shorter than a twelve bar blues, depending on where you start on it, but it’s still time. It is…

834.t: Free improvisation: Karl Berger, Braxton and the tightrope of freedom
834.s: Reacting to quotes, he sets up structures, records short miniatures, and says free playing demands serious ideas; listeners and players may hear differently, e.g. Evan Parker.
834.q: I understand that quite well. I like to have, if it’s quote unquote free improvisation, whatever that means – I like to have the settings where it’s still I don’t want to say controlled like but I kind of am controlling it as a composer setting up a certain structure or guidelines for in the moment…

525.t: Can you go beyond Ascension; Banff workshop and approach
525.s: Weiss says nobody sets out to innovate, recalls Banff under Dave Holland with Muhal Richard Abrams, and says the Cookers' approach matters most, as Billy Hart's comment on records shows.
525.q: No, I’m half kidding, but half kind of acknowledging. I think what happens is I don’t think anybody really tried to be an innovator. I think a lot of it was just natural growth. And the interesting thing is a friend I work with came back from Banff. I went to Banff right out of college. It’s a jazz…

372.t: The Capitol sessions and free playing on 'Intuition'
372.s: He recalls the executives' reluctance, how the free pieces were prepared at Lennie's house, and free playing in concert.
372.ch: The Tristano group and leaving for Kenton
372.q: He was in the booth. Whenever there was any reference that Lennie made to the people in the booth, I don’t know that he mentioned Pete Rugalo, but it sounded like there was some real executives in there that were horrified at the thought [of] playing totally free like that. Somehow it got accepted…

228.s: McLean says he cannot recall the piece and tries only to let the music evolve.
228.ch: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
228.q: I can’t remember that piece. I don’t remember it right now. So I couldn’t relate to it unless I heard it. But yeah, it wasn’t like going anywhere except just developing the music and making the music change with your mind and with your feeling for sound and rhythm. So that’s all I’ve ever tried to…

67.t: Recording with Beaver Harris and free playing
67.s: On the From Ragtime to No Time album he found free playing means forgetting conventional changes, workable but hard on the mind.
67.ch: Latin bands, Wilbur DeParis and Goodman
67.q: -- yes, the thing about it, you have to remember that you have to forget -- you have to forget the conventional changes that are played in American traditional music, you have to forget that. And you just have to throw it out of your mind altogether. Because of the music -- the bop type of music…
